source_adaptation: The owner specifies prepared contrasting source cards inside the pack. Use three cards per occupation: a broad role guide, one sample vacancy and one worker account. All are invented teaching texts, dated 30 October 2026. They offer different perspectives but are not independently verified real-world sources. The exercise practises source selection, comparison and questions; it cannot establish current pay, entry rules or actual vacancies. Real locations are replaced with generic work settings. Preserve the exact outcome and record this boundary.
success: Use at least two labelled source cards for each of two occupations.
Compare a similarity and an important difference with card evidence.
Keep one unanswered question for each occupation.
threads: Thread tags: SMSC S/So (M/C: none); British Values IL/MR (D/RL/T: none).
prepare: Books, pens, the six prepared cards, vocabulary mat and normal reading or typing aids. Keep the adult answer key apart from first responses. A calculator is optional for comparing figures; no calculation is required. No web, login or pupil phone is needed.
activity: Retrieve source/date/limit. Model a source check. Compare prepared guides, sample vacancies and worker accounts. Research both occupations using seven profile fields and source labels. Give a similarity, difference and useful questions. Feedback, fade prompts and reflect.

evidence.description: Two occupation profiles with source record: at least two labelled cards per occupation; seven requested fields or explicit gaps; one supported similarity, one important difference and one unanswered question per occupation. Keep actual support and any revision.

evidence_detail: Two occupation profiles with source record: at least two labelled cards per occupation; seven requested fields or explicit gaps; one supported similarity, one important difference and one unanswered question per occupation. Keep actual support and any revision.
assessment: Week 3 is formative. Retain two job profiles and source labels beside claims, plus one similarity, one important difference and one unanswered question per job. The seven requested fields are duties, hours, salary range, location/work setting, entry, progression and typical working conditions. A documented gap is honest research. Record missing fields and supplied answers; never fill a gap by invention. The single source end check is not the whole outcome.
boundaries: All six source cards are authored practice examples. Salary figures are invented gross annual ranges for sample posts with the same paid weekly hours. They do not show actual market rates or take-home pay. No real region, employer, organisation, qualification or entry rule is named. Different worker accounts describe different posts; they neither disprove nor verify the sample vacancy. Do not rank people or work by pay. No personal financial disclosure or final career decision. Follow the usual safeguarding route if needed.
feedback: VF verbal feedback; WS worked with support; I independent; NS next step in the same colour, on the same page or usual mode; // self-edit; ? read this back to me; E evidence recorded; R responded. Give one precise next step. R requires Voice and Audience, NS and the learner’s response in the same colour, on the same page or usual mode. A private adult can be the audience. Use E only when actual evidence is banked.
response_modes: Work in the book by default. Type instead is an optional equivalent record with the same fields and demand. Reader, scribe, speech, pointing and typing remain normal access. No pupil phone or login needed.

routes.Independent: Research both occupations with the structured field list. Use at least two source cards per occupation; the third can add or challenge a first view. Record card labels beside claims, all seven fields or explicit gaps, a similarity, an important difference and one unanswered question for each job. Explain how the source type limits a claim.
routes.Supported: Read one card and one field at a time. Use the separate model, vocabulary bank and highlighted source labels. Start with A1/A2 and B1/B2. Rehearse the comparison privately. Keep both occupations and more than one source for each. Fade answer prompts where secure, retaining normal access.
routes.Floor: Use the short choices with the source cards in view. An adult may read the cards and scribe the learner’s own choices. Point to at least two sources for each job. Choose or state a similarity, difference and an unanswered question for each job. Record uncompleted profile fields and supplied answers separately. One occupation or one source alone is partial evidence, not the full outcome.

adaptations.Cognition and Learning: Use explicit instruction, a separate model and guided practice. Chunk by occupation, source and field. Keep labels beside notes. Reuse the same question routine. Allow extra processing time and a one-card view.
adaptations.Communication and Interaction: Pre-teach occupation, source, duties, hours and entry. Rehearse privately. Accept speech, pointing, reader, scribe or typing. Ask short questions and wait. No cold calling or compulsory pair talk.
adaptations.SEMH: Use a predictable sequence and private feedback. No household pay, job history or fixed career choice required. A learner may be unsure and keep a question. Offer a regulation break with a planned return.
adaptations.Sensory and Physical: Use clear print, one-card views and usual reading or input aids. No colour-only clues. Keep a calm, uncluttered space. Do not infer whether a learner can do a role from the sample work conditions.
adaptations.EAL: Plan in any language. Check duties and entry with a concrete example. Offer oral rehearsal and short frames. Separate language access from the learner’s comparison and reasoning.

hinge: A2 lists weekday shifts for one stockroom post. A3 describes weekends in a different post. Which claim fits? A: One card must be false. B: Different posts can have different shifts, so check the post you mean. Answer B. Ask for both card labels. If insecure, underline “one post” and “different post”, re-model the scope, then use the parallel hinge.
parallel_hinge: B2 is a weekday example; B3 describes evenings in a different post. Can we claim every reception job has the same hours? A: Yes. B: No; the cards describe different examples. Answer B. Ask what to check next: the exact shifts for the particular post. Retain supported work and log uncertainty if the distinction remains insecure.
prompt_ladder: 1. Point to the place or instruction. 2. Ask a short question. 3. Rephrase the instruction. 4. Provide a scaffold or choice. 5. Model the first step only, then return the task.
frames: F: “Card ... says ... . The other card adds ... .” M: “Both roles ... . One difference is ... . Cards ... and ... show this.” H: “This source only shows ... . I still need to ask ... before using it for a real choice.”
misconceptions: “Two cards must prove a fact is true for all jobs.” Several examples still have limits; check purpose, scope, agreement and gaps. “An unanswered question means the research failed.” A precise gap is useful. Name what evidence is missing instead of guessing.
ta_focus: I do: check source label, date, type and scope. We do: ask for a card clue rather than choose the answer. Independent: record access and actual answer prompts; fade prompts when secure. Support a calm return after a break and rehearse the next research question.
accreditation: Staff confirm any accredited mapping from actual work. No criteria or unit completion inferred.

source_cards.purpose: Give a broad view of the role
source_cards.text: Checks goods when they arrive. Counts items and puts them in the right place. Reads labels and keeps stock records. The work is in a stock area with shelves and goods. It can mean standing, reaching and moving items with the right aids. In this example, entry starts with basic reading and number skills, then training for the tasks. Pay and hours depend on the post. Next steps may include stock records or guiding a small team.
source_cards.limit: A broad guide cannot give the terms of one job.
source_cards.status: Invented teaching source; prepared inside this pack

source_cards.text: One stock site. Check goods, count items and log stock. The post has 35 paid hours a week, on day shifts from Monday to Friday. Gross pay is £26,000–£29,000 a year before deductions. Training is provided for agreed tasks. Ask which aids and training are available. Work includes time on your feet.
source_cards.limit: This is one offer. It does not show the terms of all stockroom jobs.
source_cards.status: Invented teaching source; prepared inside this pack

source_cards.text: In a different post, the worker checks stock and helps the team when goods arrive. Some shifts fall at weekends. It can be noisy. They use aids and follow the agreed plan to move items. They like seeing the stock area in order.
source_cards.limit: One view does not speak for all workers. It gives no pay range or entry rule.
source_cards.status: Invented teaching source; prepared inside this pack

source_cards.purpose: Give a broad view of the role
source_cards.text: Greets visitors, checks bookings, answers messages and passes questions to the right person. Keeps clear records. The work is at a front desk or in a shared office. It may mix sitting and standing. Busy times mean switching tasks. In this example, entry starts with clear speech, reading and basic digital skills, then training for the system. Next steps may include admin tasks or guiding a desk team.
source_cards.limit: This guide cannot give the terms of one job. Pay and hours depend on the post.
source_cards.status: Invented teaching source; prepared inside this pack

source_cards.text: One front desk. Greet visitors, check bookings and pass on messages. The post has 35 paid hours a week, in the day from Monday to Friday. Gross pay is £25,000–£28,000 a year before deductions. Training is provided for agreed tasks. The worker can use a seat at the desk and may stand to greet people.
source_cards.limit: This is one offer. It gives no exact start time or promise of a next role.
source_cards.status: Invented teaching source; prepared inside this pack

source_cards.text: In a different post, the worker covers some evenings. They greet visitors and check bookings. They enjoy helping people. Busy times can bring several questions at once. They ask the team for help when needed. Some of the work involves keeping records up to date.
source_cards.limit: One view does not speak for all workers. It gives no pay range or entry rule.
source_cards.status: Invented teaching source; prepared inside this pack

paragraphs_in_document_order: Tuesday 17 November 2026 · P3 · 40 minutes · Year A
GROW · up to five learners · Independent is the default
Unit: Identity & Belonging — Belonging in work
Thread tags: SMSC S/So (M/C: none); British Values IL/MR (D/RL/T: none).
I can research two occupations from more than one source and identify similarities, differences and unanswered questions.
Weekly outcome: Students research job tasks, conditions, pay, entry routes and progression using reliable sources.

Source of record: specialist Careers scheme, GROW Careers, physical row 11, Autumn 2 row 3. E11 weekly outcome; F11 focus; G11 exact outcome; H11 sequence; I11 timing; J11 evidence; K11 access; L11 support; M11 end check; N11 formative.
How can several sources help us compare two jobs and spot what we still need to ask?
1. Use at least two labelled source cards for each of two occupations. 2. Compare one similarity and one important difference with card evidence. 3. Keep one unanswered question for each occupation.

Books, pens, the six prepared cards, vocabulary mat and normal reading or typing aids. Keep the adult answer key apart from first responses. A calculator is optional for comparing figures; no calculation is required. No web, login or pupil phone is needed.

The owner specifies prepared contrasting source cards inside the pack. Use three cards per occupation: a broad role guide, one sample vacancy and one worker account. All are invented teaching texts, dated 30 October 2026. They offer different perspectives but are not independently verified real-world sources. The exercise practises source selection, comparison and questions; it cannot establish current pay, entry rules or actual vacancies. Real locations are replaced with generic work settings. Preserve the exact outcome and record this boundary.
This helps me compare work using evidence and ask useful questions before making a career choice.
Recall a source label, date and limit from Week 2. Neutral fallback: a sample card gives one example, not every job.
Explain the three source types. Check A2 label, date, purpose and scope. Model a short profile note and an unanswered question. Check what one vacancy can show.
Use A1/A2 and B1/B2 to compare tasks and hours. Read A3/B3 for another view. Use the main and parallel hinges; explain why different posts can have different shifts.

Research both occupations from at least two cards each. Record all seven fields with labels, or a clear gap. Give a similarity, an important difference and one unanswered question per occupation. Feedback then fade answer prompts.
Ask for one important difference backed by cards. Review source use and both questions. Keep the first response, any change and next research action in the Careers Portfolio/action plan.
Total 40 minutes. Source checks, reading, vocabulary, feedback and access pauses sit within these phases. Slide 11 is an access reference; slide 12 is hidden for staff.

A2: “This is a sample vacancy, dated 30 October 2026. It describes one invented stockroom post. I can record 35 paid hours, weekday day shifts, and £26,000–£29,000 gross a year. A1 adds a possible next step in stock records or guiding a team. I still need the exact shift start time.” Point to each card label. The date tells us when the teaching card was prepared; it does not verify a real job.

Fade to B2: ask the learner to find the hours and source label, then let them use B1 to add a different detail. Retain usual reading or scribing access as answer prompts fade. The final comparison must remain the learner’s own.

Ask privately: Does A2 give the hours for one example post or every stockroom job? Which other card could add a broader view? Expected: one post; A1 adds broad tasks and possible next steps. If unclear, point to the source type and model one bounded note again.

Research both occupations with the structured field list. Use at least two source cards per occupation; the third can add or challenge a first view. Record card labels beside claims, all seven fields or explicit gaps, a similarity, an important difference and one unanswered question for each job. Explain how the source type limits a claim.

Read one card and one field at a time. Use the separate model, vocabulary bank and highlighted source labels. Start with A1/A2 and B1/B2. Rehearse the comparison privately. Keep both occupations and more than one source for each. Fade answer prompts where secure, retaining normal access.

Use the short choices with the source cards in view. An adult may read the cards and scribe the learner’s own choices. Point to at least two sources for each job. Choose or state a similarity, difference and an unanswered question for each job. Record uncompleted profile fields and supplied answers separately. One occupation or one source alone is partial evidence, not the full outcome.

Use explicit instruction, a separate model and guided practice. Chunk by occupation, source and field. Keep labels beside notes. Reuse the same question routine. Allow extra processing time and a one-card view.
Pre-teach occupation, source, duties, hours and entry. Rehearse privately. Accept speech, pointing, reader, scribe or typing. Ask short questions and wait. No cold calling or compulsory pair talk.

Use a predictable sequence and private feedback. No household pay, job history or fixed career choice required. A learner may be unsure and keep a question. Offer a regulation break with a planned return.
Use clear print, one-card views and usual reading or input aids. No colour-only clues. Keep a calm, uncluttered space. Do not infer whether a learner can do a role from the sample work conditions.
Plan in any language. Check duties and entry with a concrete example. Offer oral rehearsal and short frames. Separate language access from the learner’s comparison and reasoning.
Normal access does not automatically change the academic route. Log answer prompts separately from reading, scribing, typing or other usual aids.

A2 lists weekday shifts for one stockroom post. A3 describes weekends in a different post. Which claim fits? A: One card must be false. B: Different posts can have different shifts, so check the post you mean. Answer B. Ask for both card labels. If insecure, underline “one post” and “different post”, re-model the scope, then use the parallel hinge.

B2 is a weekday example; B3 describes evenings in a different post. Can we claim every reception job has the same hours? A: Yes. B: No; the cards describe different examples. Answer B. Ask what to check next: the exact shifts for the particular post. Retain supported work and log uncertainty if the distinction remains insecure.

F: “Card ... says ... . The other card adds ... .” M: “Both roles ... . One difference is ... . Cards ... and ... show this.” H: “This source only shows ... . I still need to ask ... before using it for a real choice.”

I do: check source label, date, type and scope. We do: ask for a card clue rather than choose the answer. Independent: record access and actual answer prompts; fade prompts when secure. Support a calm return after a break and rehearse the next research question.
1. Point to the place or instruction. 2. Ask a short question. 3. Rephrase the instruction. 4. Provide a scaffold or choice. 5. Model the first step only, then return the task.

“Two cards must prove a fact is true for all jobs.” Several examples still have limits; check purpose, scope, agreement and gaps. “An unanswered question means the research failed.” A precise gap is useful. Name what evidence is missing instead of guessing.

J11: Two-job research profiles with source record. M11: Can the student identify one important difference between the two researched occupations? Check this difference with card evidence, then check the full outcome separately: two occupations, at least two sources each, a similarity, a difference and unanswered questions.

Week 3 is formative. Retain two job profiles and source labels beside claims, plus one similarity, one important difference and one unanswered question per job. The seven requested fields are duties, hours, salary range, location/work setting, entry, progression and typical working conditions. A documented gap is honest research. Record missing fields and supplied answers; never fill a gap by invention. The single source end check is not the whole outcome.

Work in the book by default. Type instead is an optional equivalent record with the same fields and demand. Reader, scribe, speech, pointing and typing remain normal access. No pupil phone or login needed.

VF verbal feedback; WS worked with support; I independent; NS next step in the same colour, on the same page or usual mode; // self-edit; ? read this back to me; E evidence recorded; R responded. Give one precise next step. R requires Voice and Audience, NS and the learner’s response in the same colour, on the same page or usual mode. A private adult can be the audience. Use E only when actual evidence is banked.

Keep the first comparison, source record, actual support and any revision in the Careers Portfolio/action plan. Offer to the Communication portfolio. Staff confirm any accredited mapping from actual work; no unit completion is inferred. Keep one question as a next research action.
Teaching need next lesson ____________________ Next research action ____________________

All six source cards are authored practice examples. Salary figures are invented gross annual ranges for sample posts with the same paid weekly hours. They do not show actual market rates or take-home pay. No real region, employer, organisation, qualification or entry rule is named. Different worker accounts describe different posts; they neither disprove nor verify the sample vacancy. Do not rank people or work by pay. No personal financial disclosure or final career decision. Follow the usual safeguarding route if needed.

Exact outcome: I can research two occupations from more than one source and identify similarities, differences and unanswered questions.
Check goods, count and store items, read labels and log stock (A1/A2).
A2: 35 paid hours, weekday day shifts. A3: some weekends in a different post.
A2: invented £26,000–£29,000 gross annually, before deductions, for 35 paid weekly hours.
Stock area with shelves (A1); one stock site (A2). No real location.
A1: basic reading/number skills then task training. A2: training for agreed tasks. No exact qualification stated.
A1: possible stock-record work or guiding a small team. No guaranteed next role.
Standing, reaching and moving items with aids (A1); time on feet (A2); noise and agreed movement plan in one account (A3).

Useful open questions: exact shift start time; which aids are available; content and length of training. A named post description or purposeful question to someone responsible for that post would be a later source. Do not make contact during this lesson.
Greet visitors, check bookings, pass messages, keep records (B1/B2).
B2: 35 paid hours, weekday daytime. B3: some evenings in a different post.
B2: invented £25,000–£28,000 gross annually, before deductions, for 35 paid weekly hours.
Front desk/shared office (B1); one front desk (B2). No real location.
B1: clear speech, reading, basic digital skills then system training. B2: training for agreed tasks. No exact qualification stated.
B1: possible admin tasks or guiding a desk team. No promised next role in B2.
Mix of sitting and standing, switching tasks (B1); seat/standing to greet (B2); several questions at busy times (B3).

Similarity: both sample vacancies have 35 paid weekly hours and weekday daytime work (A2/B2); both role guides include keeping records (A1/B1). Difference: stockroom tasks focus on goods while reception tasks focus on visitors and bookings (A1/B1). Typical settings and sample pay ranges also differ, with scope stated.

If comparing pay: both are gross annual ranges for the same paid weekly hours. The ranges overlap from £26,000 to £28,000. It is unsupported to say every stockroom worker earns more than every reception worker. No pay calculation is needed.

Useful reception questions: exact start time; what training covers; which system is used; whether this particular post has any evening shifts. A question should identify a gap rather than repeat a point already stated.

Recall source label, date and a limit from the previous illustrative-data task. If missed, use “one sample vacancy describes one post”. After the model, expected answers are one post, and A1 for broad tasks or possible progression. A recent date alone is not a trust guarantee.

Locate label/date/type/purpose. Decide what the source actually covers. Check a specific claim against another card and note gaps. The prepared cards deliberately give different views: general tasks, a particular offer and one person’s experience. Their consistency within this teaching set is checked; no external validation is claimed.
B is supported: A2 weekdays and A3 weekends describe different posts. Ask for both labels and the words that show scope. If insecure, re-model those words and use the parallel hinge.

B is supported: B2 weekday work and B3 evenings cannot justify one rule for all reception jobs. A useful next check is the exact shifts of the particular post. Retain supported work and record uncertainty if needed.

Two cards do not automatically establish a universal fact. Their purpose, coverage and relationship matter. Different examples are not necessarily a contradiction. An unanswered question is useful when it identifies missing evidence. “Not stated” is preferable to an invented detail.

Floor key A, A, A, B, A, B. The choices check sources, one similarity, one difference and two gaps. They do not alone supply all profile fields. Keep actual responses and prompts. Accept alternatives supported by the cards. Read or scribe faithfully without supplying conclusions.

J11 calls for two-job research profiles with source record. The exact outcome requires two occupations, more than one source, similarities, differences and unanswered questions. In this pack, collect at least two card labels for each occupation, one supported similarity, one important difference and one useful unanswered question per occupation. Record the seven profile fields from H11 or explicit gaps. The narrower M11 difference check is not proof of the complete outcome.

Secure: “A2 and B2 both give 35 paid hours. A1 handles goods; B1 greets visitors. A1/A2 and B1/B2 give my profiles. I still need the exact stock shift start and the reception training details.” Check that the profiles carry the seven fields or honest gaps. Partial: one job, one card for a job, an unreferenced comparison or missing questions. Unsupported: “All these jobs have the same hours”.

“Add a second card for reception.” “Put the card label beside your hours claim.” “Name what differs about the tasks.” “Choose a question the cards leave open.” Give one next step, then retain the learner’s response.

Reader, scribe, typing and normal aids do not automatically reduce independence of thought. Record answer prompts separately. Fade prompts where secure, without removing access. No cold calling or compulsory public performance.

Prepared teaching sources dated 30 October 2026. All posts and accounts are invented. They do not describe real vacancies, pay or entry rules.
Purpose: Give a broad view of the role.

Checks goods when they arrive. Counts items and puts them in the right place. Reads labels and keeps stock records. The work is in a stock area with shelves and goods. It can mean standing, reaching and moving items with the right aids. In this example, entry starts with basic reading and number skills, then training for the tasks. Pay and hours depend on the post. Next steps may include stock records or guiding a small team.
Limit: A broad guide cannot give the terms of one job.

One stock site. Check goods, count items and log stock. The post has 35 paid hours a week, on day shifts from Monday to Friday. Gross pay is £26,000–£29,000 a year before deductions. Training is provided for agreed tasks. Ask which aids and training are available. Work includes time on your feet.
Limit: This is one offer. It does not show the terms of all stockroom jobs.
Purpose: Show one invented worker’s view.

In a different post, the worker checks stock and helps the team when goods arrive. Some shifts fall at weekends. It can be noisy. They use aids and follow the agreed plan to move items. They like seeing the stock area in order.
Limit: One view does not speak for all workers. It gives no pay range or entry rule.
Prepared teaching sources dated 30 October 2026. All posts and accounts are invented. They do not describe real vacancies, pay or entry rules.
Purpose: Give a broad view of the role.

Greets visitors, checks bookings, answers messages and passes questions to the right person. Keeps clear records. The work is at a front desk or in a shared office. It may mix sitting and standing. Busy times mean switching tasks. In this example, entry starts with clear speech, reading and basic digital skills, then training for the system. Next steps may include admin tasks or guiding a desk team.
Limit: This guide cannot give the terms of one job. Pay and hours depend on the post.

One front desk. Greet visitors, check bookings and pass on messages. The post has 35 paid hours a week, in the day from Monday to Friday. Gross pay is £25,000–£28,000 a year before deductions. Training is provided for agreed tasks. The worker can use a seat at the desk and may stand to greet people.
Limit: This is one offer. It gives no exact start time or promise of a next role.
Purpose: Show one invented worker’s view.

In a different post, the worker covers some evenings. They greet visitors and check bookings. They enjoy helping people. Busy times can bring several questions at once. They ask the team for help when needed. Some of the work involves keeping records up to date.
Limit: One view does not speak for all workers. It gives no pay range or entry rule.
A2 gives one stockroom post: 35 paid hours a week, in the day from Monday to Friday. A1 adds a possible next step in stock records or guiding a team. I still need the exact shift start time.
The note uses A2 and A1 for different details. It does not claim all stockroom jobs are the same.
Research stockroom assistant and reception assistant. Use at least two cards for each. Start with A1/A2 and B1/B2. A3/B3 add another view.
Use these headings: duties; hours; salary range; place of work; entry; next steps; work conditions. Add a card label to each point. Write “not stated” for a real gap.
Give one similarity and one important difference. Back each with card labels. Keep one unanswered question for each job. Say what source could help answer it next.
What is its label and date? Is it a guide, one vacancy or one account? What is its purpose? What can it tell me? What does it leave out? Does another card add to it?
A date alone does not prove a claim. Different examples may have different hours. Check the post you mean.

Keep the cards in view. An adult can read them. Use both jobs and at least two card labels for each.

weekly_plan_row.objective_verbatim: I can research two occupations from more than one source and identify similarities, differences and unanswered questions.
